# Is 1000 a Good SAT Score in 2026? Percentiles & Next Steps


## TL;DR


A 1000 SAT score sits at roughly the 47th percentile among recent SAT takers and falls slightly below the 2025 national average of 1029. It is not competitive for selective colleges, but it can work at many accessible universities where 1000 falls within the admitted-student score range. The smartest next step is to compare your score against each target school’s middle 50% SAT range, then decide whether to submit it, retake, or apply test-optional.


> **Quick Answer: Is 1000 a Good SAT Score?**
>
>
> A 1000 SAT score is slightly below the current average and around the middle of the SAT score distribution. It can be a workable score for many colleges, but it is generally not competitive at highly selective universities. The most important question is where 1000 falls within each college’s reported SAT range. If it is within or above the middle 50%, submitting it may make sense. If it is below the 25th percentile at a test-optional school, retaking or applying without the score may be the better choice.
>
>
> **In short:** A 1000 is not a bad SAT score, but whether it is a good score depends on your target colleges, GPA, coursework, scholarship goals, and whether you can realistically improve with another attempt.


## Is a 1000 SAT Score Good in 2026?


A 1000 SAT score puts you around the middle of the SAT score distribution, but whether it is “good” depends on the colleges you want to attend. For some universities, 1000 falls comfortably within the reported SAT range for enrolled students. For selective colleges, it is usually well below the typical range.


The more useful question is not whether 1000 is good in isolation. It is whether 1000 is competitive **for your target schools** and whether submitting it will strengthen your application.


If you already have a 1000, compare your score with each college’s 25th and 75th percentile SAT scores. That comparison can tell you whether to submit your score, apply test-optional, or retake the SAT.


If you are considering a retake, start with a diagnostic to identify which section and question types are limiting your score before spending more time studying.


## What Does a 1000 SAT Score Mean?


The SAT is scored on a scale from 400 to 1600. It has two sections: Reading and Writing (200 to 800) and Math (200 to 800). Your total score is the sum of those two section scores. The digital SAT, which replaced the paper version, uses[the same scoring scale](https://satsuite.collegeboard.org/sat/whats-on-the-test/structure) , so a 1000 on the digital SAT carries the same meaning as a 1000 on the old paper test.

**Important:** These labels are general context, not admissions guarantees. A college's own SAT range is more useful than a national label when deciding whether your score is competitive.


A 1000 sits near the bottom of that middle band. Most prep guides would not call it a good SAT score, but it is not in the range that closes doors everywhere either. For a broader view of where different scores land, see our[guide to good SAT scores](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/what-is-a-good-sat-score-guide) .


One thing most articles skip: the same 1000 total can come from very different section splits. A student who scored 550 Reading and Writing / 450 Math has different strengths and prep needs than someone who scored 460 Reading and Writing / 540 Math. The total score tells you where you are. The section scores tell you why.


## What Percentile Is a 1000 SAT Score?


College Board publishes two types of percentiles. The nationally representative percentile compares your score against a research sample of all U.S. 11th and 12th graders, including students who never took the SAT. The user group percentile compares it against students who actually sat for the test in recent years.


Measure


1000 SAT Score


Nationally representative percentile


48th percentile


SAT user-group percentile


47th percentile


Approximate position among recent SAT takers


Around the middle


Interpretation

A 1000 SAT score is therefore roughly in the middle of the distribution. You scored higher than approximately 47% of recent SAT test takers, while about 53% scored higher.


A 1000 SAT score lands at the 48th nationally representative percentile and the 47th user group percentile. In plain English, scoring 1000 means you performed about as well as, or better than, roughly 47% of recent SAT takers.


That is why calling 1000 “terrible” is misleading. You outperformed close to half of everyone who took the test. But “middle range” is not the same as “competitive,” especially for schools that attract higher-scoring applicants. Our[SAT percentiles guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-percentiles-user-vs-national-guide) explains the difference between these two percentile types in more detail.


## Is 1000 Above or Below the National Average?


Below, but barely. College Board’s 2025 Total Group SAT Suite Annual Report puts the mean SAT score at 1029, based on just over 2 million test takers from the 2025 graduating class. The mean section scores were 521 for Reading and Writing and 508 for Math.

A 1000 is only 29 points below the 2025 SAT-taker mean, so it is better described as **slightly below average rather than dramatically below average** .


A 1000 is 29 points below that mean. That is a small gap, not a chasm. Still, “slightly below average” is a more honest label than “average.”


Some competing websites list the average SAT score as “1050 to 1100.” That figure is outdated. If you are trying to figure out whether 1000 is a good SAT score, use the 1029 figure from the latest official report as your reference point.


## What the 1000-point total does not tell you


A 1000 SAT score alone cannot show whether you meet both section-level college-readiness benchmarks. Because the Reading and Writing and Math benchmarks are evaluated separately, your section scores matter.


For example, two students can both score 1000 but have very different academic profiles:


-


550 Reading and Writing + 450 Math


-


500 Reading and Writing + 500 Math


-


470 Reading and Writing + 530 Math


-


450 Reading and Writing + 550 Math


The total score is identical, but the section-level strengths and weaknesses are different. If you plan to retake the SAT, use your section scores to decide where additional preparation is most likely to produce points.


Score Split


Benchmark Status

Meets RW benchmark (480), misses Math benchmark by 30


470 RW / 530 Math


Meets Math benchmark, misses RW benchmark by 10


530 RW / 470 Math


Strong RW, larger Math gap of 60 points


450 RW / 550 Math


Meets Math benchmark, needs 30 more points in RW


This is not trivia. Your section split tells you exactly where to focus if you decide to retake. A student with 500 Math needs different prep than one with 550 Math, even though both scored 1000 overall.

A 1000 is not universally good or bad. At UHD, it is right in the middle. At the University of North Florida, it falls below the 25th percentile and would be a weaker data point. ## Is a 1000 SAT Score Good for Different Types of Colleges?


A 1000 SAT score can mean very different things depending on the type of college you are targeting. Instead of treating 1000 as universally good or bad, compare it with the typical SAT range at the schools on your list.

The key takeaway is simple: **a 1000 is more useful when it falls inside your target college's reported SAT range.**


## Is 1000 Good Enough for Selective Colleges?


Usually, no.


Selective colleges report median SAT scores well above 1300, and the most competitive schools report medians in the high 1400s to 1500s. A 1000 is hundreds of points below those ranges.


If your target is a school where the 25th percentile SAT is 1300 or higher, a 1000 will not help your application. At test-optional selective schools, applying without a score is almost always a better strategy than submitting one that falls far below the school’s range.


That said, a 1000 SAT score does not mean you cannot go to college. It means your realistic college list should include schools where 1000 falls within range. Plenty of solid universities fit that profile.

College counselors on LinkedIn recommend this school-by-school approach. One counselor advises students to pull each college’s Common Data Set, compare their score to the middle 50% range, and note what percentage of admitted students actually submitted scores. If fewer than half submitted and your score is below the 25th percentile, the score is unlikely to strengthen your file.


Another counselor suggests that students unsure about submitting should contact admissions offices directly and ask whether a lower score could hurt under their test-optional policy. Schools will not make the decision for you, but they sometimes share useful policy-specific guidance.

## Should You Retake the SAT After Scoring 1000?


Often, yes. But only if a higher score would actually change something, like getting into the middle 50% at a target school, qualifying for a merit scholarship, or meeting a section benchmark.


**Retake if:**


-


Your target schools’ 25th percentile SAT scores are above 1000


-


A gain of 50 to 150 points would put you inside the middle 50% at several colleges


-


One section score is clearly below the College Board benchmark (480 RW, 530 Math)


-


You have enough time before the next test date to study with a real plan


-


A scholarship or honors program uses SAT scores


**Skip the retake if:**


-


Your schools are test-free or test-optional and your GPA tells a stronger academic story


-


You are already inside the score range at your realistic target schools


-


Deadlines are close and your time is better spent on essays and recommendations


-


Practice scores have stayed flat after focused prep


College Board says[most students improve](https://bigfuture.collegeboard.org/help-center/can-i-retake-sat) when they retake after first sitting for the SAT in spring of junior year. A 2017 study of nearly 250,000 students found that 20 hours of personalized practice was associated with an[average 115-point gain](https://newsroom.collegeboard.org/new-data-links-20-hours-personalized-official-sat-practice-khan-academy-115-point-average-score) . That data is older and the result is associative, not a guarantee. But it shows that targeted prep can meaningfully move a score.


For a student at 1000, the most practical first target is 1050 to 1150, not 1500. A 100-point gain can shift several colleges from “below range” to “in range.”


## How to Improve From a 1000 SAT Score


Improvement starts with understanding what went wrong, not just grinding through random practice questions.


### Step 1: Diagnose the Split


Look at your section scores. Is your weakness Math, Reading and Writing, or both equally? A student with 550 RW / 450 Math has a clear priority. A student sitting at 500/500 needs a broader approach.


### Step 2: Compare to Benchmarks


Use College Board’s readiness benchmarks as your first targets: 480 for Reading and Writing, 530 for Math. If you are below either one, that section is your starting point. Once you clear both, push toward 550 or 600 in each.


### Step 3: Use Targeted Practice


Practitioners on Reddit consistently recommend official-style question bank practice over passive video watching. One student preparing to retake from a 1000 said timing was the biggest problem, and other users advised working through timed question sets before jumping into full-length exams.


The[Miyagi Labs question bank](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/question-bank) includes filters by domain, skill, and difficulty, which makes it easier to focus on weak areas instead of studying everything at once.


### Step 4: Keep an Error Log


For every missed question, record:


-


The question type


-


Why the wrong answer was tempting


-


The correct concept or rule


-


Whether it was a content gap, timing issue, misread, or careless error


Patterns will emerge fast. Most students around the 1000 level have a handful of recurring mistake types, not dozens of different problems.


### Step 5: Retest When Practice Scores Move


Do not sign up for a retake out of hope. Retake when your practice test scores consistently hit your target range. If your goal is 1100, you should be scoring 1080 to 1120 on timed practice tests before sitting for the real exam. For a full study framework, see our[plan to improve by 200 points](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-to-improve-sat-score-by-200-points-5-step-plan) .


## The Emotional Side of Scoring 1000


This part does not get discussed enough in score guides.


Students on Reddit describe a 1000 in wildly different emotional terms. One student posted that they were “glad” to hit 1000 because they had never reached it before, and the score proved they were not “dumb” at standardized tests. For that student, 1000 was a milestone. Another described their 1000 as “painfully mediocre” and planned to retake with a target around 1150.


Both reactions are valid. Threads on r/ApplyingToCollege show the same split: some users remind students that not every school is a top-20 institution and that a 1000 with a decent GPA still opens paths, while others are less generous.


Here is the honest take. A 1000 SAT score does not define your intelligence. It tells you where your current SAT performance stands on one test, on one day. That is a data point, not an identity.


## Is a 1000 SAT Score Enough for Scholarships?


Sometimes, but it depends on the school and the specific award.


Some universities factor SAT scores into merit aid decisions. At a school where 1000 is above the typical student profile, it might contribute positively. At a school where the average admitted student scored 1200, a 1000 will not move the needle for competitive awards.


College Board notes that even test-optional colleges may use scores for scholarships, placement, or academic support, separate from the admissions decision itself. So even at a school that does not require scores for admission, sending a 1000 might matter for a specific funding opportunity.


The general rule: a higher score expands merit aid options. If scholarship money is a priority and you have time, improving from 1000 to 1100 or 1150 could have financial returns beyond just admissions.


## The Test-Optional Factor


According to FairTest, over 1,940 of the 2,089.html?v=1) four-year bachelor’s-granting colleges it tracks are test-optional or test-free for fall 2026. That is a large majority. But “test-optional” does not mean “scores are irrelevant.” It means you choose whether to submit.


For a student asking whether 1000 is a good SAT score, this is actually helpful. You can apply without your score at schools where it falls below range, while still submitting it at schools where it fits. This school-by-school strategy is the practical middle ground between “always submit” and “never submit.”


Some schools have also moved back toward requiring scores. The situation is not uniform and changes year to year, so check each school’s current policy directly before you decide.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is a 1000 SAT score bad?


Not exactly. A 1000 is slightly below the 2025 SAT-taker average of 1029 and sits at about the 47th percentile among recent test takers. “Middle range” or “slightly below average” is more accurate than “bad.” It is weak for selective colleges but usable at schools where it falls within the admitted-student score range.


### Can I get into college with a 1000?


Yes. Many colleges enroll students with SAT scores around 1000 to 1100. Check each school’s Common Data Set or published score ranges to see whether 1000 falls inside their middle 50%.


### Should I retake the SAT if I scored 1000?


Retake if a realistic score increase of 50 to 150 points would move you into the middle 50% at target schools or help with scholarship eligibility. Skip the retake if your schools are test-free, or if your time is better spent strengthening other parts of your application.


### Can I raise a 1000 to 1200?


Many students can, but it requires targeted study, not just more hours. Historical College Board data found 20 hours of personalized practice was associated with a 115-point average gain, and some students gained 200 points or more. A jump from 1000 to 1200 is achievable with focused work, though not automatic.


### Should I go test-optional with a 1000?


At schools where 1000 is below the 25th percentile of admitted students, going test-optional is usually stronger, especially if your GPA and coursework tell a better academic story than your test score.


### What if my section scores are very uneven?


An uneven split (like 580 RW / 420 Math) means your total score hides a specific weakness. Focus prep on the lower section first. Gaining 50 to 80 points in one section is often faster than trying to move both sections by smaller amounts.


### Is 1000 good for a first SAT attempt?


It is a reasonable starting point. Most students who take the SAT as juniors improve on a retake, especially with targeted study between attempts. A first score of 1000 gives you a clear baseline and specific areas to work on.


## What to Do Next


If you scored 1000 and are not sure what comes next, start with two things.


First, compare 1000 against the middle 50% SAT range at every school on your list. That single comparison will tell you whether to submit, withhold, or retake.


Second, if a retake makes sense, do not guess at what to study. Take a diagnostic to identify which skills and question types cost you the most points, then build a focused plan around those gaps.
